resources.string: Convert SWR, reflection coefficient magnitude and return loss, or calculate them from load impedance.
SWR describes load matching. Antenna efficiency also depends on losses within the antenna.
Use R and X measured at the same point. Positive X is inductive; negative X is capacitive. An SWR value alone cannot determine impedance or reflection phase.
Enter a complete number using a decimal point or comma, up to 32 characters. Scientific notation is not supported.
Complete the selected inputs to see the result.

The model assumes a passive load and a positive real reference impedance. All results refer to the same reference plane. Both waves attenuate as they travel through the cable, so the SWR at the transmitter may be lower than at the load. Account for feedline attenuation when assessing the match at the antenna.

The upper arrow shows the incident wave traveling from source to load. The lower arrow shows the reflected wave. Together they form a standing wave. Voltage SWR is the ratio of its maximum to minimum amplitude. Arrow lengths are illustrative.
Power balance at an SWR of 2:1

This example is at the load reference plane. With 100 W incident, the load accepts 88.89 W and reflects 11.11 W. Return loss (RL) is the ratio of incident to reflected power (9.54 dB). Mismatch loss (ML) is the reduction in accepted power caused by reflection (0.51 dB). Cable attenuation is calculated separately. Accepted power includes power dissipated within the load.
How the load affects transmitter power

At an SWR of 2:1, mismatch loss is 0.51 dB at fixed incident power. A mismatch can also cause the transmitter to reduce the incident power. In that case, the power accepted by the antenna can drop by more than 0.51 dB compared with matched operation. The impedance at the transmitter output, the electrical length of the feed line, and the transmitter protection can all affect the result.

In this example, the amplifier delivers 100 W into 50 Ω. The RMS limits at the load are about 1.414 A and 70.71 V. The current is limited by the lower of the current limit and the voltage limit divided by |Z|. The power delivered to the load is I² × R, where R is the resistive part of the impedance.
Voltage at 70.71 V, current falls to 0.71 A

The 25 Ω load is limited by current, and the 100 Ω load is limited by voltage. Each receives 50 W, down 3.01 dB from the matched load. The 40 + j30 Ω load receives 80 W at the same SWR. These values already account for mismatch.

If the power accepted by the transmitting antenna is halved, received power drops by 3.01 dB as long as the transmitting antenna gain toward the receiver, the receiving system, and the propagation conditions stay the same. SWR alone cannot predict actual transmitter output or received signal level.
Gamma equals load impedance minus reference impedance, divided by their sum.
SWR equals one plus the magnitude of gamma, divided by one minus its magnitude.
Return loss equals minus twenty times the base-ten logarithm of the magnitude of gamma.
Reflected power fraction equals the squared magnitude of gamma. Mismatch loss equals minus ten times the base-ten logarithm of one minus that fraction.
